text: Gridlock is a standstill where nothing moves because everyone blocks everyone else. It began as a traffic term and now describes a government unable to pass laws. Here, split control of Washington makes a freeze look likely.
A concession is something you give up in a negotiation to reach a deal. Here, some Democrats want Mr Trump to give more ground before they back a bill on building power plants.
A loyalist is someone who stays faithful to a leader or cause. Here it means an ally Mr Trump would like to place on the Federal Reserve's board, which a Democratic Senate could block.
A knack is a natural talent or clever skill for doing something. Here Mr Trump is good at squeezing his politics into catchy four-letter slogans.
Emblazoned means displayed boldly and prominently, as on a banner or shirt. Here the red caps carry the MAGA slogan in big letters.
To thump someone in sport or politics means to beat them heavily. Here the Republicans lost badly in the midterm elections.
Elections held halfway through a president's four-year term, in which all House seats and about a third of Senate seats are contested. The president's party often loses ground.
Short for 'Make America Great Again', Mr Trump's campaign slogan. Supporters wear red caps with the letters.
Latin for 'I forbid'. A veto is a president's power to reject a bill so that it cannot become law unless Congress overrides it by a two-thirds vote in each chamber.
A chamber is one of the two houses of Congress: the House of Representatives and the Senate. A bill must pass both.
Sweeping means broad and far-reaching, covering a great deal. Here the tax-and-spending law changed many things at once.
Disproportionately means to a much larger degree than would be fair or expected. Here the law gave far more benefit to rich people than to others.
To swell is to grow bigger. Here the law enlarged the forecast gaps between what the government spends and what it collects.
A deficit is the gap in a year when a government spends more than it collects in taxes. It covers the gap by borrowing.
Actions a president can take alone, without a new law from Congress, such as setting tariffs or directing immigration enforcement.
Deportation is the legal removal of a person from a country, usually someone who lacks permission to stay.
A deadline is a date by which something must be done. Here two budget dates force Congress and the president to negotiate.
A short-term stopgap that keeps government funding at current levels for a few weeks or months, pushing the real fight to later.
A legal cap on how much the US Treasury may borrow in total. Hitting it without a fix risks a default on bills already owed, so it is a potent bargaining chip.
In finance, to default is to fail to pay a debt on time. A US default would shake markets around the world. Not to be confused with a computer's default setting.
A classic economics trade-off between spending on the military ('guns') and on civilian needs ('butter'). The article says America's usual answer is both.
A US tax benefit that tops up the pay of low-income workers. The article calls it a 'top-up for low earners'.
A US tax break that reduces what a family owes for each child. Democrats want to expand it.
An idiom for losses or deficit spending, from the old habit of recording losses in red. Here it means how much more the government will borrow.
Fiscal means relating to government spending and taxes, as opposed to monetary policy, which is about interest rates and the money supply.
Fiscal loosening means the government spends more or taxes less, adding to the economy. Here it is estimated at 0.2% of GDP.
Gross domestic product, the total value of everything a country produces in a year. It is the standard yardstick of an economy's size.
The US government health-insurance programme for people with low incomes, funded jointly by the federal government and the states.
The common name for the US food-assistance programme that helps low-income families buy groceries.
To offset is to balance out one thing with an opposite one. Here, tax or spending changes elsewhere would cancel part of the new cost.
A levy is a tax or charge imposed by a government. Here Democrats might put a new charge on the AI industry.
Giant buildings full of computers that store data and run AI systems. They use enormous amounts of electricity.
An informal phrase for going full speed with no restraint. Here it describes Mr Trump's hands-off approach to regulating data centres.
Capacity is the maximum amount something can produce or hold. Here it means the data-centre capacity planned across states.
A research group that studies policy and advises politicians. Third Way is described as centre-left.
Changing the approvals process for building things like power plants and power lines so projects get approved faster.
The high-voltage cables that carry electricity from power plants to cities and towns.
To shoulder a cost is to take on responsibility for paying it. Here large data centres would pay more of what they cost the power grid.
The grid is the connected network of power plants and lines that supplies a region's electricity.
Tariffs are taxes on imported goods. They raise prices for buyers and are a central part of Mr Trump's economic policy.
Literally an exit from a highway. Figuratively, a face-saving way out of a policy or conflict. Here a court ruling could let Mr Trump ease tariffs without seeming to back down.
A US trade law letting the government punish other countries for unfair trade practices with tariffs. A pending court case could limit such duties.
The freedom to choose between options. Here Mr Trump's freedom of action may shrink as Democrats gain power.
America's central bank, which sets interest rates. Its independence from politics is seen as important for stable prices.
A strict campaign of enforcement against people living in the country without permission.
Undocumented describes a person living in a country without legal papers or permission. Here, long-term workers who have been in America many years.
A senior Trump adviser known as a main architect of the hardline deportation campaign, now named White House chief of staff.
Short for 'Trump Always Chickens Out', a market-trader joke that he backs down from threats such as tariffs. Here it is set against VETO as the likelier path.
